diagrams.title: One front door for every model call
diagrams.summary: Two team apps send calls to one gateway. The gateway checks the key, looks up the alias, calls a provider, records the tokens and cost, and returns the answer. If a provider fails, a gateway can try another one.

steps.caption: Every team sends its calls to the same front door. A call carries an alias and a key, never a provider name or a provider key.
The gateway checks that the key is allowed in, then looks the alias up in its table.
It calls the provider behind that alias, using a provider key that only the gateway holds.
The provider answers and reports how many tokens it read and wrote.
The gateway writes one row to its log: which alias, how many tokens, what it cost.
The answer goes back to the app that asked. The app learned nothing about providers or keys.
Meant to: if provider one fails, the gateway retries on provider two and the app never notices. The lab's copy does not do this.

diagrams.title: One name, many models
diagrams.summary: A team calls the alias support. The gateway looks it up, forwards the call to the model behind it and returns the answer.

steps.caption: The app asks for the alias support. It never names a provider or a model.
The gateway looks the alias up. Two deployments exist, and support points at a.
The call goes to deployment a. Deployment b is not involved.
The answer comes back the same way. Change the alias table and the app never notices.

diagrams.title: Every call leaves a receipt
diagrams.summary: A team app calls the gateway. The model answers with a usage count, the gateway prices it and writes one row to the spend log, and finance reads that log by team.

steps.caption: The app sends a chat request with its team key. The key tells the gateway who is asking, even though the request body does not.
The gateway forwards the call to the model behind the alias.
The model answers and reports how many tokens it read and wrote. Tokens are what providers charge for.
The gateway multiplies tokens by the price for that model and writes one row: who called, which alias, which model, tokens and cost.
The answer goes back to the app. The caller never sees the price, but the record now exists.
Finance reads the log and adds rows up by team. A call that leaves no row is spend nobody can explain.

diagrams.title: When the provider says no
diagrams.summary: A provider returns a 503 to the gateway. The gateway records the failure and returns a clean error that tells the caller the request was fine but the upstream failed.

steps.caption: A perfectly good request arrives at the gateway.
The gateway forwards it to the provider behind the alias.
The provider is overloaded and answers 503. Nothing was wrong with the request. The provider simply cannot serve it right now.
The gateway knows this is a failure on the far side, not a mistake by the caller, and it records the failed attempt.
The caller gets an error in the same shape as any other API error. It is a server-side status, not a made-up success and not a hang.
Because the status says whose fault it was, the app can retry later or switch alias instead of rewriting a request that was fine.

diagrams.title: Saving is not the same as loading
diagrams.summary: An engineer adds a model alias to the config file. The running gateway keeps its old table until it reloads, so the first call fails and a call after the reload works.

steps.caption: An engineer adds the alias translate to the config file and saves it. The file on disk now knows about it.
The gateway read the file when it started and keeps that table in memory. Saving the file did not touch the running process.
A team calls translate right away. The gateway checks its table, finds nothing and rejects the call.
The engineer reloads the gateway, so it reads the file again. Only now does the new line take effect.
The table in memory now has translate. The same call that failed a minute ago succeeds, and the app changed nothing.

diagrams.title: A menu of tools, in one language
diagrams.summary: An agent asks a tool server what it offers, gets a menu with names and input shapes, lets the model choose, calls the tool with matching inputs and gets a result back.

steps.caption: The agent connects to a tool server and asks what tools it has. Every MCP server answers this same question the same way.
The server replies with a menu: each tool has a name, a plain description and the inputs it expects.
The agent shows the model the user question and the menu. The model decides a tool would help and picks one.
The agent sends the call in the shape the menu promised, with the order id filled in.
The tool server does the real work against the system behind it. The agent never needs to know how that system is reached.
The result travels back in the standard shape, and the model turns it into an answer for the user.

diagrams.title: One door, many tool servers
diagrams.summary: An agent talks to one virtual server. It bundles chosen tools from three tool servers, hides the ones that should not be exposed and routes each call to the server that owns the tool.

steps.caption: The agent has one address and one key. It asks the hub what tools it can use.
Behind the hub sit three tool servers. The virtual server is a list that picks tools from each of them.
One tool on the admin server is risky, so the bundle leaves it out. The agent cannot see it, let alone call it.
The agent calls a docs tool. It uses the same address as before and does not know which server owns the tool.
The hub routes the call to the docs server and passes the result back.
Add or move a server later and only the bundle changes. The agent keeps the same address and never needs new wiring.

diagrams.title: A tool that fails still answers
diagrams.summary: A tool call reaches the tool server, but the API behind it times out. The server wraps the failure in a normal reply flagged as an error, so the agent can read it and decide what to do.

steps.caption: The agent calls get_invoice through the hub, with a valid invoice number.
The hub finds the tool server that owns the tool and passes the call on.
The tool server asks the invoice API for the record.
The API takes too long and the server gives up. The call was delivered fine. The work behind it failed.
The tool server does not crash the connection. It returns a normal reply with an error flag set and a short message.
The agent reads the flag and the message. It can retry, try another tool or tell the user honestly what went wrong.

diagrams.title: Fetch the pages first, then answer
diagrams.summary: Documents are stored ahead of time as vectors. A question goes to the retrieval service, which asks the store for the nearest chunks with scores and hands them, with the question, to the model that writes the answer.

steps.caption: Ahead of time, each document is cut into chunks. Each chunk is turned into a vector, a list of numbers, and saved in the store.
Later a question arrives. The model has never read your documents, so it cannot answer from memory.
The service turns the question into a vector with the same function and asks the store for the closest chunks.
The store returns the top-k nearest chunks, each with a similarity score. It ranks them, it does not judge them.
The service hands the question and those chunks to the model. Only the chunks go into its context window, not the whole corpus.
The model writes its answer from the chunks it was given. If they were the wrong chunks, the answer is fluent and wrong.

diagrams.title: Meaning as numbers
diagrams.summary: Documents and a question pass through the same embedding model. Each becomes a list of numbers, and the vector index returns the chunks whose numbers point in the most similar direction.

steps.caption: Ahead of time, every document is cut into chunks and each chunk goes through an embedding model.
Each chunk is stored as a vector, a list of numbers. Chunks that mean similar things get vectors that point in similar directions.
Later a question arrives as plain text.
The same model turns the question into a vector. Using the same model matters, or the numbers would not be comparable.
The index compares the question vector with the stored ones and picks the closest. Similar meaning is close, even when no words match.
The best chunks come back ranked, each with a similarity score.

diagrams.title: How close is close enough
diagrams.summary: The index returns its five nearest chunks with scores. A cutoff keeps the ones that are similar enough, drops the rest and passes only the kept passages to the answering model.

steps.caption: A question goes to the vector index.
The index always returns its nearest chunks, however weak. Here it finds five, each with a score from 0 to 1.
The cutoff compares each score with a threshold the team chose. Scores at or above it stay.
Two hits fall below the line and are dropped. Close matches survive, weak ones do not.
Only the kept passages go to the answering model, so it works from evidence that is on topic.
Set the cutoff too high and good passages vanish. Set it too low and noise gets in. It is a dial to tune against real questions.

diagrams.title: When the answer is not in the documents
diagrams.summary: A question the documents do not cover still gets a nearest hit from the index, but the hit scores low on an unrelated topic. The cutoff rejects it and the model says it does not know.

steps.caption: A customer asks about something the company never wrote down.
The index cannot say nothing. It returns whatever is nearest, and that chunk is about a different subject.
The nearest hit is on its way with a low score of 0.34. Nearest does not mean relevant.
Without a cutoff this chunk would reach the model, which would build a confident answer on the wrong document. With one, nothing passes.
The model is told there is no supporting text, and it can answer honestly that this is not in the documents.
An honest I do not know costs the customer a moment. A confident wrong answer with a citation costs their trust.

diagrams.title: A request, drawn as spans
diagrams.summary: One request passes through a service that calls a database and a model. Each step is timed as a span, and the tracing backend joins the spans into one trace with a shared id.

steps.caption: A request arrives at the service. It opens a span, a timed record of one piece of work, and gives the whole request a trace id.
The service reads from the database. That is a smaller span inside the first, with its own start and duration.
Then it calls the model. This span is much wider than the others, which is exactly what a trace is for: it shows where the time went.
Every span ends and carries the same trace id. The service sends the finished spans to the tracing backend.
The backend groups spans by trace id and shows one request as a timeline you can read from top to bottom.

diagrams.title: Passing the thread along
diagrams.summary: A trace continues across services only when each call carries the trace context. A hop that drops it starts a separate trace, so the parent and child link is lost.

steps.caption: The gateway starts a span for the request. It has no parent, so it is the root of the trace.
The gateway calls the worker and adds a header with the trace id and the id of span A. This header is the thread that ties services together.
The worker reads the header and opens its span as a child of A, in the same trace.
The worker calls storage and passes the header on again, this time naming B as the parent.
Now suppose a hop forgets the header. Storage has no context, so it starts a brand new trace.
Every hop has to read the context it receives and send it on. Then one request reads as one tree: A above B above C.

diagrams.title: Putting a price on a span
diagrams.summary: A model call is a span. The gateway copies the token counts, model and cost onto it as attributes, so finance can total spend by team straight from the traces.

steps.caption: The app calls the gateway, and the gateway opens a span around the model call.
The model answers and reports its usage: tokens read and tokens written.
The gateway writes the facts onto the span as attributes: the model name, the token counts, the cost and the calling team.
The finished span, attributes included, is exported to the trace backend with the rest of the request.
Finance can now filter and add up attributes across many traces. Answering who spent what needs no new code in the app.

diagrams.title: Onboarding a team, step by step
diagrams.summary: A new team files one request. The portal records the team and its budget, then gives the gateway a scoped key and the tool hub a tool bundle, and hands the team a key and starter docs.

steps.caption: A team files one request: who they are, what they will build and which region their data may use.
The portal creates the team record with an owner, a monthly budget and a region. Everything after this hangs off that record.
It asks the gateway for a key limited to the aliases the team needs. The team does not get keys to everything.
It also gives the tool hub a bundle of the tools this team may call, and nothing more.
The team receives its key and starter docs. Each step was done by the platform, so no one works from a checklist on a wiki page.

diagrams.title: A key is a list of names
diagrams.summary: A key lists the aliases it may call. A call inside the list goes through, a call outside it is refused, and a legacy alias only works once the platform adds it to the key.

steps.caption: The team app calls the alias chat with its key. The gateway reads the key and the list of aliases it is scoped to.
Chat is on the list, so the call goes through to the model behind it.
An older service of the same team still calls chat-v1, the name from before a rename.
Chat-v1 is not on the key list, so the gateway refuses before any model is called. The key was valid, but its scope did not cover that name.
The platform keeps chat-v1 as a legacy alias pointing at the same model and adds it to the scope. Now the old name works.
Scopes list names, not models. Keep legacy names alive, with an owner, until every caller has moved to the new one.

diagrams.title: Prove it works from the team side
diagrams.summary: A smoke test acts as the new team with its real key. It makes one model call, one tool call and one retrieval call, then confirms the usage row for the team exists.

steps.caption: Checking settings is not enough. The test uses the new team key, the same way the team will, and tries each thing they were promised.
First a model call through the gateway with a real alias. A reply proves the key, the alias and the route line up.
Next a tool call through the hub. A reply proves the tool bundle was attached and the key is allowed to use it.
Then a retrieval call. A passage from the team documents proves the index exists and the key can reach it.
Last, the spend log. A row for this team proves the call was recorded against the right budget.
One failed leg says exactly what to fix. When all four pass, the team is ready and you can prove it.

diagrams.title: Routes decide where data may go
diagrams.summary: Each deployment sits in one region. A route ties an alias to the regions it may use, so personal data stays on an EU route while a public question may use either region.

steps.caption: The app sends a request that contains customer details, using the alias for personal data.
The gateway looks up the route for that alias. The rule says EU only.
The request goes to the EU deployment. The US one is never contacted, however busy or cheap it is.
Now a request about a public product page, sent through a different alias. Its route allows both regions.
For this route the gateway may pick either deployment, so it uses the US one.
A region belongs to a deployment. A route is the rule that says which regions a kind of data may use.

diagrams.title: The log sees one hop, the trace sees all
diagrams.summary: A request passes through a regional proxy before it reaches the provider. The spend log records only the first hop, while a trace records every hop, so an audit needs the trace.

steps.caption: A request enters the gateway. An auditor may ask later where this exact request went.
The gateway does not call the provider directly. Its route sends the call to a regional proxy first.
The proxy forwards the call to the provider. The gateway is not involved in this second hop.
The spend log records what the gateway saw: one destination, the proxy. It says nothing about what happened after that.
Each hop also reports a span to the trace store with the same trace id, so together they form one chain of custody.
To prove where data went, read the trace, which covers every hop. The log is good for money but blind past the first hop.

diagrams.title: What the label says, what happened
diagrams.summary: A route declares EU, but when the EU provider is busy the regional proxy overflows the call to a US provider. The answer looks normal, and only the actual region on the trace shows the difference.

steps.caption: The app sends a customer request on a route that is declared EU.
The gateway follows the declaration and sends the call to the proxy that is labelled EU.
The proxy tries the EU provider, but it is at capacity and refuses.
To keep the service up, the proxy quietly overflows to a US provider. The call has left the declared region.
The answer returns as usual. Nothing in the reply or the label shows that anything changed.
Declared is what the config promises. Actual is where the call really went. Compare the region on each span of the trace, not the label on the route.

diagrams.title: One request, one trace id
diagrams.summary: The gateway starts a trace and passes its id to every service it calls. Each service times its own work as spans and sends them to the tracing backend, which joins them into one trace.

steps.caption: A request reaches the gateway. It makes a trace id, a label that belongs to this one request, and opens the first span.
The gateway calls the model worker and sends the trace id along with the call. The worker opens its own span.
Then the gateway calls the vector store, with the same id. The store opens a span of its own.
The vector store calls the cache and passes the id on again. That span records the store as its parent.
Every service sends its finished spans, with start, end and id, to the tracing backend.
The backend groups the spans by trace id and draws one timeline. No one had to line up four logs by hand.

diagrams.title: One platform, shared by every team
diagrams.summary: A team calls one gateway with its own key and one tool hub for its tools. Both sit in front of the models and tool servers, and every call leaves a record of who made it and what it cost.

steps.caption: The team has one address to learn for models and one for tools. It does not choose providers or keep provider keys.

notes.text: one key, issued to the team

steps.caption: The team's app calls the gateway with a model alias. The key says which aliases this team may use.
The gateway checks the key, then sends the call to the model behind the alias.
When an agent needs a tool, it asks the tool hub. The hub offers only the tools bundled for this team.
The hub passes the call to the tool server that owns the tool and returns the result.
Both doors write to the same place, so a question like who spent this has one place to look.

diagrams.title: A prompt is data that travels
diagrams.summary: A support ticket becomes a prompt, and the prompt is processed by a provider in some region. The contract names a region, and only a record kept as the request ran can prove which one it was.

steps.caption: A support ticket holds a customer's name, order and complaint. As soon as it goes into a prompt, that text is personal data.
The app sends the prompt to the gateway. The gateway decides which provider will process it.
The provider reads the prompt and writes the answer. From here the customer's data is being processed in that provider's region.
The customer's contract names a region. A different provider could have been used, and the answer would look the same.
So each service the request touches records that it was there, and in which region. Kept together, those records are the audit trail.
Rules and config files state what should happen. The trail shows what did, which is what an auditor can sign.
